claims.text: Applying a thin nickel layer to tungsten particles before W–Cu composite fabrication will lower interfacial thermal resistance.
Applying a thin nickel layer to tungsten particles will improve mechanical bonding at the W–Cu interface.
The nickel interlayer will increase the thermal conductivity of W–Cu relative to a comparable untreated W–Cu composite.
The nickel interlayer will retain or enhance the mechanical durability of W–Cu.
The nickel interlayer will retain or enhance the irradiation resistance of W–Cu.
The proposed baseline is a conventionally fabricated composite of tungsten particles embedded in a copper matrix with untreated tungsten surfaces.
The intervention is physical-vapor deposition of a nickel interlayer tens of nanometers thick on tungsten particles before composite fabrication.
The coated composite is to be liquid-phase sintered at 1100–1200 °C under a reducing atmosphere.
Processing will produce a continuous, Ni-rich interfacial layer between tungsten and copper.
The Ni-rich interfacial layer will create a graded transition between tungsten and copper.
Nickel acts as a wetting agent that improves W–Cu interfacial contact.
The graded nickel-containing interface reduces electron scattering at the W–Cu interface.
The graded nickel-containing interface reduces phonon scattering at the W–Cu interface.
Reduced interfacial electron and phonon scattering produces more efficient heat transfer.
The nickel-containing interface reinforces mechanical cohesion.
The nickel-containing interface improves resistance to radiation-induced damage.
The predicted benefit is intended to hold under cyclic thermal loads and irradiation conditions typical of fusion-reactor joints.
Coating uniformity, interlayer thickness, and sintering conditions may affect the effectiveness of the intervention.
